debate.situation: Your friends are buying homes or getting married, and you feel behind even though you are not sure you want those things. You have reported two things: the feeling of lag, and real doubt about the goals. What you have not said is what the lag feels like, whether it is about missing out on a life, losing closeness with friends, money, or simply being measured. That unknown matters most, because each answer points to a different next step.

minds.title: The Status Anthropologist
minds.concern: Whether the feeling of being behind comes from the social ladder rather than from your own wants.
minds.author: Thorstein Veblen
minds.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class

minds.title: The Experimenter
minds.concern: Learning what you want by trying small, reversible things instead of deciding by introspection.
minds.author: Herminia Ibarra

minds.title: The Forecasting Skeptic
minds.concern: How badly people predict what will make them happy, including predicting that something will not.
minds.author: Daniel Gilbert

debate.speaker: The Status Anthropologist
debate.text: Start with the odd part: you feel behind in a race you are not sure you entered. That sounds like comparison, not desire. Veblen called it "invidious comparison": we rank ourselves against peers whether or not we want their prizes. Your doubt about the goals may be the more trustworthy signal.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Too fast. Not sure I want it is not the same as I do not want it. People often decide who they are by thinking, then discover they were guessing. Sit and ponder and you get a confident story. Run small tests and you get data.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: You both sound sure of yourselves, which worries me. Anthropologist, you are forecasting that these lives would not suit them. Experimenter, you are forecasting that tests will reveal it. We are bad at predicting our future feelings. The best evidence is people who actually live the thing, and I would ask them.
debate.author: Daniel Gilbert
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness

debate.speaker: The Status Anthropologist
debate.text: Ask the friends, sure, but they are the least neutral witnesses. Their reports are filtered by the same pressure: nobody announces the mortgage was a mistake at the housewarming. I grant that surrogates beat introspection. I narrow it: ask many, ask in private, ask the quiet ones.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Skeptic, you cannot trial-run a marriage. Fair. But these milestones are bundles. Housing is roots, space, equity. Marriage is commitment, a partner, shared life. Each piece has a cheap version: renting longer-term somewhere, hosting dinners, a serious relationship. Test the pieces, not the ceremony.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Accepted, with a warning: tests have the same bias. A short trial of settled life may feel flat simply because it is new, or lonely because you did it alone. Now the fact I would want. When you feel behind, is it envy of their lives, fear of drifting from them, or worry about money? Each one changes what you do.
debate.author: Daniel Gilbert
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness

debate.speaker: The Status Anthropologist
debate.text: I will bet on the second. Friends moving into a shared script means fewer shared evenings, and the sting is exclusion, not ambition. If so, the milestones are a symptom and the remedy is ordinary: keep your friendships alive on different terms. I would go further than Veblen here. That is my extension, not his claim.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: I would not bet. It could equally be real longing wearing a comparison costume, and you only find out by acting. Notice what is in conflict here: freedom and belonging. Maybe security as well. I will not rank them. That ranking belongs to you, and trials would show which one hurts when you give it up.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Here is the case for doing nothing. Many people are only behind for a stretch, and the feeling fades as plans change. Waiting costs little if no clock is truly running. But I will concede a point to the Anthropologist: a persistent feeling is still information about something, even if it is not information about marriage.
debate.author: Daniel Gilbert
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness

debate.speaker: The Status Anthropologist
debate.text: Then we have shifted. I no longer say the feeling is false, only that it is a poor guide to what you want. The Experimenter says act small, the Skeptic says ask people who have done it. I still dispute whether the true target is the milestones at all or the friendships around them.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the feeling of being behind and the question of what you want are two separate things, and one cannot settle the other. Not being sure you want the milestones does not mean you do not, and the sting may be about comparison, belonging, or something you have not named. What stays disputed is whether the real source is social exclusion or an unacknowledged wish for some version of settled life. One possible reflection: when you imagine the feeling gone, what is left that you would still want?
debate.dependsOn: If the feeling is mostly about drifting from friends, then keeping those friendships alive on new terms is more reasonable than changing your life plan, because the milestones are not what is missing. If it eases when you picture a quieter, unconventional life but returns when you picture living alone for years, a small trial of one piece of settled life (a longer-term home, a serious relationship) becomes more reasonable, because the cost is low and you learn something real. If money or a genuine deadline is the pressure, then practical planning matters more than self-examination, because the constraint is outside your preferences. If you cannot tell which applies, a proportionate way to learn is to talk privately with a few people who have taken these steps and note what they say they gained and gave up, and to watch for a few weeks which of your reactions persist.
